section_path: Article
text: Engineering lipid nanoparticle surface hydrophobicity to modulate nano-bio interface and enable tissue-selective mRNA delivery

section_path: Abstract
text: Predominant liver accumulation remains a major challenge for the application of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based gene therapies. While tuning the apparent pKa is an effective strategy for influencing endogenous proteins that regulate LNP-mediated tissue-specific delivery, recent evidence suggests that alternative mechanisms may exist. Here, we reveal a new mechanism by which LNP surface hydrophobicity influences extrahepatic delivery. Using dendrimers as modular molecules and an in-house developed surface hydrophobicity assay, we show that reducing lipid grafting on the dendrimer decreases the surface hydrophobicity of dendrimer-based LNPs (dLNPs), leading to reduced stability in plasma and decreased plasma protein adsorption. This diminishes the ability of LNPs to target liver hepatocytes through endogenous mechanisms involving interactions between apolipoproteins and their cognate receptors. At the same time, we find that dLNPs with lower surface hydrophobicity exhibit enhanced targeting of granulocytes relative to monocytic cells, potentially due to complement protein interactions. Further modification of dendrimers with quaternary amines increases dLNP surface charge density and improves lung delivery by preferentially targeting lung epithelial cells. While this modification also reduces surface hydrophobicity, the enhanced lung delivery is associated with distinct protein corona compositions rather than reduced protein adsorption. These findings establish modulation of LNP surface hydrophobicity as a novel strategy for achieving extrahepatic delivery.

section_path: Introduction
text: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) represent the most clinically advanced non-viral system for the delivery of RNAs, including messenger RNA (mRNA) and small interfering RNA (siRNA). To date, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved four LNP-based therapeutics: Comirnaty, Spikevax, mRESVIA, and Onpattro. Among these clinical products, Onpattro is the only therapeutic that utilizes systemic administration as the route of delivery [1]. Although LNPs can be a promising tool for the delivery of nucleic acids for protein replacement therapy [2], gene editing [3], and in situ cell therapy [4], these therapeutic applications are limited by LNPs’ predominant liver accumulation, particularly in liver hepatocytes, upon systemic delivery [5,6]. Developing strategies to control the tissue tropism of LNPs therefore remains a central challenge in the field.

section_path: Introduction
text: Upon systemic administration, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) rapidly shed their surface-bound polyethylene glycol (PEG) lipids [7]. This is followed by the adsorption of plasma proteins, resulting in the formation of a dynamic “protein corona” around the LNPs [7]. These interactions can compromise the structural integrity of the LNPs, potentially leading to lipid dissociation, particle agglomeration, and premature release of RNA [7,8]. At the same time, protein adsorption plays a critical role in mediating cellular uptake and in vivo biodistribution. For example, in the case of Onpattro, the adsorption of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) onto the LNP surface facilitates recognition by low-density lipoprotein receptors (LDLR) on hepatocytes, thereby promoting receptor-mediated endocytosis and efficient liver delivery of RNA cargos [6,7,9–11]. Building on this endogenous mechanism, engineering approaches have been developed to control the tissue-specific delivery of RNA. Specifically, tuning the apparent pKa of the lipid-based delivery system serves as a simple and effective method for manipulating the endogenous proteins that govern their subsequent tissue-specific delivery towards the liver, spleen, or lung [11–13]. Despite the success of this design principle emerging evidence has shown the apparent pKa might not be the only factor that affects the extrahepatic delivery of LNPs. Engineering the chemical structures of the ionizable lipids, particularly the lipid tails, can also enhance extrahepatic delivery without significantly altering the apparent pKa of LNPs [14–23]. As a result, predicting the biodistribution of LNPs from the chemical structure of ionizable lipids remains elusive. These findings indicate that additional physicochemical properties of LNPs contribute to their interactions with plasma proteins and their subsequent in vivo biodistribution.

section_path: Introduction
text: The surface hydrophobicity of a nanoparticle has significant effects on its stability, biological absorption, transportation, and distribution [24]. Previous studies have shown the hydrophobicity of nanoparticles can impact both the quantity and quality of plasma protein adsorption [25]. For example, polymeric nanoparticles with higher hydrophobicity tend to exhibit enhanced plasma protein adsorption [26–28]. PEGylation of the nanoparticle surface decreases the surface hydrophobicity and consequently reduces protein adsorption [29,30]. Earlier studies of liposomes have demonstrated that the structure of phospholipids significantly influences the liposome’s hydrophobicity and membrane fluidity, which in turn affects the types and amounts of plasma components that bind to their surface in vivo [30–33]. Specifically, compared to saturated, longer-chain phospholipids, unsaturated, shorter-chain phospholipids lead to less rigid and less hydrophobic membranes. These loosely packed membranes are more susceptible to apolipoprotein partitioning and lipid exchange with endogenous lipoproteins like high-density lipoproteins (HDLs), ultimately compromising liposome structural integrity and thereby reducing circulation half-life [32,34–36]. These prior studies offer valuable insights into how LNP hydrophobicity influences cellular uptake and tissue-specific delivery via interactions with plasma proteins.

section_path: Introduction
text: Here, we report a new mechanism through which reduced LNP surface hydrophobicity can mediate extrahepatic delivery. Using dendrimers as modular scaffolds, we constructed a library of dendrimerbased lipid nanoparticles (dLNPs) with tunable lipid grafting densities that systematically modulate nanoparticle hydrophobicity. Structure–function analysis revealed that decreasing lipid grafting reduced dLNP surface hydrophobicity and significantly altered plasma protein adsorption. Reduced hydrophobicity diminished apolipoprotein-mediated hepatocyte uptake, resulting in decreased liver mRNA expression compared to conventional LNPs. Instead, low-hydrophobicity dLNPs preferentially transfected splenic myeloid cells, which correlated with enrichment of complement proteins and immunoglobulins in the protein corona and enhanced targeting of granulocytic populations. Furthermore, conversion of dendrimer amines into permanently cationic quaternary amines further reduced hydrophobicity and altered surface charge, producing a distinct protein corona composition that enabled efficient mRNA delivery to lung epithelial cells. Together, these findings expand the current framework of LNP design beyond apparent pKa and establish hydrophobicity tuning as a rational strategy for engineering extrahepatic RNA delivery.

section_path: Results > Construction of structurally diverse dLNPs for in vitro screening
text: Motivated by the unique structural properties of dendrimers, we constructed structurally diverse lipid-grafted poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM) dendrimers for the formulation of mRNAs into dLNPs (Fig. 1A). First, we selected six amine cores (C1–C6), which underwent iterative Michael addition with methyl acrylate and amidation with ethylenediamine to generate dendrimers of different generations (G0, G1, and G2). Next, we functionalized the dendrimers by grafting their terminal amine groups with four lipid epoxides differing in chain length (L8, L12) and structure (branched LB, unsaturated UNL). To modulate lipid grafting, we adjusted the epoxide lipid-to-dendrimer ratio, yielding dendrimers with 0%, 50%, or 100% lipid modification. These variations resulted in dendrimers with distinct surface amine compositions: primary amines (0% grafting), secondary amines (50%), and tertiary amines (100%) (see Supplementary Information 1 for synthesis details). Overall, we synthesized 162 lipid-grafted dendrimers by systematically varying amine core structures, dendrimer generations, lipid types, and grafting percentages. These dendrimers were then co-formulated with helper lipids and mRNAs to generate dLNPs (Fig. 1A). Most formulations exhibited consistent particle sizes between 80 nm and 200 nm, polydispersity index (PDI) between 0.1 and 0.3, and zeta potential between −0.5 mV and 0 mV (Supplementary 3, Fig. S1A–C). To identify optimal dLNP formulations for in vivo biodistribution studies, we screened for transfection efficiency and relative cell viability in RAW264.7 cells. Given that the protein corona significantly affects cell type-specific uptake of LNP, in vitro screening was performed under serum-free conditions to minimize bias induced by cell type-specific uptake. The in vitro screening identified 10 lead dLNP formulations (Fig. 1B), which exhibited comparable potency and toxicity profiles to commercially available transfection reagents, including SM-102, DLin-MC3-DMA, DOTAP, C12-200, and jetMESSENGER.

section_path: Results > Construction of structurally diverse dLNPs for in vitro screening
text: Further machine learning analysis, integrating key dendrimer structural features with in vitro screening data, revealed that the number of lipid tails is a critical predictor of high transfection efficiency and high relative cell viability in dLNPs (see Supplementary Information 2 for details). The evaluation metrics (e.g., balanced accuracy) for relative cell viability and transfection efficiency evaluated from the developed multi-class DNN based on the 5-fold cross-validation and test set are summarized in Supplementary Information 2. AUC-ROC values for all classes in different output targets were above 0.86, indicating that the model possesses strong discriminatory power for each class, and the AUC-ROC curves are shown in Supplementary Information 2, Fig. S2. To assess whether lipid grafting affects dLNP physicochemical properties and in vitro performance, we analyzed the impact of lipid grafting across all dLNP candidates in our library. Compared to the 50%- and 100%-series dLNPs, the 0%-series dLNPs (containing dendrimers with no lipid grafting) exhibited significantly larger size, higher PDI, greater encapsulation efficiency, and improved cell viability but much lower transfection efficiency (Supplementary 3, Fig. S1A–F). No significant differences were observed in size, PDI, or zeta potential between the 50% and 100% series (Supplementary 3, Fig. S1A–C). However, in vitro studies revealed that 50% lipid-grafted dLNPs achieved higher transfection efficiency, both in average efficacy and number of successful hits (Supplementary 3, Fig. S1D). This increase in transfection efficiency was not attributable to differences in encapsulation efficiency, as 50% and 100% series dLNPs showed similar mRNA loading efficiency (Supplementary 3, Fig. S1F). Notably, serum proteins known to influence LNP cellular uptake were excluded from the in vitro experimental setup. Therefore, these findings suggest that the number of lipid tails plays a critical role in facilitating mRNA encapsulation, promoting endosomal escape, and enabling efficient RNA release, which represent three ratelimiting steps for successful transfection.

section_path: Results > Lipid grafting influences tissue-specific mRNA delivery
text: To evaluate the in vivo fate of lead dLNP formulations, we systemically injected luciferase mRNA-loaded dLNPs into C57BL/6 mice and performed bioluminescent imaging across major organs, including the spleen, liver, lungs, bone (femur), heart, and kidneys, 24 h post-injection. Our results showed that 9 out of the 10 injected lead dLNPs showed consistent high in vivo transfections. Interestingly, dLNPs with 100% lipid-grafted dendrimers exhibited strong liver-preferential expression, with 67%–89% of mRNA signal detected in the liver. In contrast, dLNPs with 50% lipid-grafted showed spleen-preferential expression, with 61%–86% of mRNA signal detected in the spleen (Fig. 1C, Supplementary 3, Fig. S2). Notably, the size, PDI, zeta potential, and encapsulation efficiency were not significantly different between the 100% lipid-grafted and the 50% lipid-grafted dLNPs (Fig. 1D), indicating the tissue-specific mRNA expression was not associated with these physiochemical properties. To further investigate the impact of lipid grafting on tissue selectivity, we compared two pairs of “sister formulations”, defined as dendrimers with identical core structure, generation, and lipid tail, but differing in lipid grafting percentage (50% vs. 100%) (Fig. 1E and F). This variation influenced lipid tail numbers and the ratio of secondary to tertiary amines. For example, C1G1-L8-50 and C5G0-L12-50 contained four and two lipid tails, respectively, whereas their 100% lipid-grafted counterparts contained twice as many lipid tails (eight and four). Additionally, the 50% formulations retained secondary amines, whereas their 100% counterparts contained only tertiary amines. These structural differences led to strikingly distinct mRNA distribution patterns. The 50% lipid-grafted formulations (C1G1-L8-50 and C5G0-L12-50) exhibited predominant spleen expression (85.3 ± 2.4% and 61.5 ± 7.9%, respectively). In contrast, their 100% lipid-grafted counterparts (C1G1-L8-100 and C5G0-L12-100) showed strong liver-preferential expression, with 89.2 ± 3.5% and 69.5 ± 27.6% of mRNA expression in the liver (Fig. 1E and F). These findings highlight the critical role of lipid grafting in directing mRNA delivery between the liver and spleen.

section_path: Results > Lipid grafting modifies dLNP surface properties
text: The apparent pKa is a key determinant of LNP tissue-specific delivery [11]. Given the differences in tissue mRNA expression between the 50% series and 100% series dLNPs, we first characterized the apparent pKa of the lead dLNP formulations using the TNS assay. In general, the apparent pKa for the 50% series dLNPs was slightly higher than that of the 100% series (Fig. 2A), likely due to the presence of secondary amines formed when grafting one lipid tail per terminal primary amine (Fig. 1A). The apparent pKa of the 100% series dLNPs ranges from 6.9 to 7.7 (Fig. 2A), aligning with reported values for liver-targeting formulations [5,11]. In contrast, the 50% series had an apparent pKa of 7.5 to 8.4 (Fig. 2A), which differs from the previously reported range (2 to 6) for spleen-targeting LNPs [11]. This suggests that spleen-preferential expression by dLNPs may be governed by additional mechanisms beyond apparent pKa. Further analysis revealed a correlation between higher apparent pKa and increased splenic mRNA expression, along with reduced hepatic expression. However, this trend was not consistent across the 50% and 100% series (Fig. 2B), indicating that other factors linked to lipid grafting may influence tissue distribution. Since lipid grafting alters both the amine type (secondary vs. tertiary) and the number of lipid tails per dendrimer, we investigated whether a reduced number of lipid tails affects dLNP hydrophobicity, given that ionizable lipids constitute 50% of the total lipid molar ratio and are concentrated on the LNP surface (Fig. 2C).

section_path: Results > Lipid grafting modifies dLNP surface properties
text: To evaluate LNP hydrophobicity, we developed a fluorescence probe-based assay using hydrophobic dye: 6-propionyl-2-(N,N-dimethylamino)naphthalene (PRODAN) (Fig. 2D). PRODAN has been previously used to assess protein surface hydrophobicity and was adapted for this analysis [37–41]. The absence of charged functional groups in PRODAN minimizes electrostatic interactions, while their aromatic rings enhance hydrophobic interactions, causing wavelength of maximum fluorescence emission shifts when binding to hydrophobic environment (Fig. 2E) [42]. Unlike logP, which measures the intrinsic hydrophobicity of a single chemical entity based on its partition coefficient between two solvents, the PRODAN assay reflects the global surface hydrophobicity of multicomponent nanoparticles based on the fluorescent response of PRODAN upon interacting with hydrophobic regions on the LNP surface. Therefore, we calculated the hydrophobicity index (S0) by taking the initial slope of the fluorescence intensity versus dLNP concentration plot following established method (Fig. 2F) [38,42,43]. Using this method, C1G1-L8-100 showed 3.6 times higher hydrophobicity than C1G1-L8-50 (Fig. 2F). Extending this assay to all lead dLNP formulations, we found that the 100% series dLNPs had significantly higher hydrophobicity than the 50% series (Fig. 2G, Supplementary 3, Fig. S3). Cryo-EM analysis further validated these differences, showing that C1G1-L8-100 had a conventional LNP structure with a homogeneous, multi-layered core, while C1G1-L8-50 exhibited bilayer vesicles with an electron-dense surface (Fig. 2H, Supplementary 3, Fig. S4). Additional physicochemical analysis revealed that C1G1-L8-50 had similar size and size distribution (NTA: 167.4 ± 44.3 nm; DLS: 158 ± 4.8 nm, PDI = 0.25) compared to C1G1-L8-100 (NTA: 140.2 ± 56.3 nm; DLS: 166.6 ± 2.9 nm, PDI = 0.15) (Fig. 2I), with both formulations showing similar ζ potentials (−2.4 ± 0.5 mV vs. −0.4 ± 0.4 mV).

section_path: Results > Lipid grafting modifies dLNP surface properties
text: We extended our analysis to clinical formulations to determine whether the number of lipid tails in ionizable lipids influences hydrophobicity. SM-102 contains three lipid tails, while ALC-0315 has four (Fig. 2J). When co-formulated with helper lipids and mRNAs into LNPs, both formulations showed similar apparent pKa values (7.17 ± 0.05 for SM-102 vs. 6.44 ± 0.02 for ALC-0315). However, SM-102 LNPs exhibited higher spleen mRNA expression, with 75.4 ± 10.3% of expression in the spleen and 19.9 ± 8.2% in the liver, while ALC-0315 LNPs showed higher liver mRNA expression, with 77.0 ± 12.2% in the liver and 19.7 ± 11.7% in the spleen (Fig. 2K). Hydrophobicity analysis revealed that SM-102 LNPs had 2-fold lower hydrophobicity than ALC-0315 LNPs (Fig. 2L). These findings confirm that for non-dendrimer-based ionizable lipids, the number of lipid tails also affects LNP hydrophobicity. Plotting all lead formulations based on their apparent pKa and hydrophobicity clearly grouped them according to tissue-selective delivery (Fig. 2M). Together, these results suggest that in addition to apparent pKa, LNP hydrophobicity is a critical factor in determining tissue selectivity, specifically between the spleen and liver.

section_path: Results > The hydrophobicity of dLNPs affects the quantity of plasma protein adsorption
text: It is well-established that nanoparticles interact with plasma proteins upon entering the bloodstream, forming a “protein corona” on their surface. Recent studies have highlighted a strong correlation between the protein corona and the nanoparticle’s in vivo targeting behavior. To explore how lipid grafting affects dLNP interactions with plasma proteins, we incubated two pairs of sister dLNP formulations (C1G1-L8-50 vs. C1G1-L8-100 and C5G0-L12-50 vs. C5G0-L12-100) with mouse plasma (C57BL6 plasma supplemented with K2 EDTA as anticoagulant, Innovative Research) ex vivo at 37 °C for 15 min and isolated the plasma proteins bound to the dLNPs [11,19,44]. Quantification of proteins isolated from blank plasma showed a minimal protein amount (1.04 ± 0.91 μg), in contrast to substantially higher protein amounts isolated from dLNP-treated plasma (ranging from 10 to 25 μg) (Fig. 3A), indicating that the majority of isolated proteins were associated with the dLNPs. Notably, significant differences in protein amounts were observed between the sister formulations. Specifically, the total amount of plasma proteins associated with the 100% series dLNPs was approximately twofold higher than that of the 50% series (Fig. 3A).

section_path: Results > The hydrophobicity of dLNPs affects the quantity of plasma protein adsorption
text: Exposure to plasma proteins, such as apolipoproteins, can compromise LNP integrity and alter protein adsorption. To assess whether differences in protein adsorption were related to the different stability of 50% and 100% series dLNPs, we tracked dLNP size distribution changes in plasma using NTA over a 3-h period, following a previously reported method [45]. A fluorescent helper lipid, TopFluor™ TMR-PC, was incorporated at 0.5% (molar ratio) to label all dLNPs, enabling accurate tracking of dLNPs in plasma with minimal background interference [45] (Supplementary 3, Fig. S5A). Control experiments confirmed that the addition of 0.5% TMR-PC did not significantly affect dLNP size (pre-labeling: 140.2 ± 56.3 nm; post-labeling: 145.5 ± 55.9 nm). In PBS, both C1G1-L8-50 and C1G1-L8-100 remained stable throughout the 3-h incubation period (Supplementary 3, Fig. S6). In plasma, both formulations showed increasing size heterogeneity over time (Fig. 3B; Supplementary 3, Fig. S5B), consistent with previous studies that showed interactions with apolipoproteins and lipoproteins in the plasma can induce LNP destabilization and aggregation [32,34–36]. Similar effects were also seen in clinical formulations based on SM-102 and ALC-0315 (Supplementary 3, Fig. S5B). Since protein corona quantification was done at 15 min after incubation, we further analyzed particle distribution change within the first 15min after plasma exposure. At 0 min, the size of C1G1-L8-50 is smaller than C1G1-L8-100, but both are narrowly distributed. After 15min incubation with plasma, both of C1G1-L8-50 and C1G1-L8-100 showed broadened size distributions (Fig. 3C). However, C1G1-L8-50 became larger and more heterogenous than C1G1-L8-100 (Fig. 3D), indicating the C1G1-L8-50 is less stable in the plasma than C1G1-L8-100. The lower plasma stability of 50% series dLNPs could stem from their lower hydrophobicity, making its lipids more flexible to exchange with lipoproteins and itself more susceptible to apolipoprotein partitioning, both of which could negatively affect the adsorption of other plasma proteins on their surface. To further validate this hypothesis in a non-dendrimer system, we analyzed the total plasma protein abundance associated with the clinically used ionizable lipids SM-102 and ALC-0315. Due to the additional lipid tail, ALC-0315-based LNPs demonstrated higher hydrophobicity than SM-102-based LNPs in our PRODAN assay (Fig. 2L). Protein mass quantification revealed that plasma proteins bound to ALC-0315 were 17.5% higher than those associated with SM-102 (Supplementary 3, Fig. S7). Similar to C1G1-L8-50, SM-102 became more heterogenous than ALC-0315, indicating SM-102 is less stable in the plasma. In conclusion, these results underscore the importance of dLNP hydrophobicity in determining their interactions with plasma proteins (Fig. 3E).

section_path: Results > The hydrophobicity of dLNPs affects the quantity of plasma protein adsorption
text: Given the observed differences in the total amount of proteins adsorbed to the 50% and 100% series dLNPs, we next examined the major composition of these adsorbed proteins. Sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) revealed that the molecular weights and relative abundance of most proteins were comparable between the two sister formulations (Supplementary 3, Fig. S8A). To further quantify protein binding, we employed unbiased mass spectrometry (MS) proteomics to analyze the relative abundance of proteins associated with C1G1-L8-50 and C1G1-L8-100. Apolipoprotein A-I (ApoA1), Vitronectin (Vtn), and Albumin (Alb) emerged as the top three most abundant proteins in both formulations, with nearly identical relative abundances (Fig. 3F,Tables S1 and S2). No significant differences in isoelectric point (pI) were observed between proteins adsorbed to C1G1-L8-50 and C1G1-L8-100 (Supplementary 3, Fig. S8B). However, a slightly higher proportion of hydrophobic proteins was associated with C1G1-L8-100 (1.88%) compared to C1G1-L8-50 (0.98%), as indicated by Grand Average of Hydropathy (GRAVY) scores (GRAVY score >0) (Supplementary 3, Fig. S8C). Collectively, these findings indicate that the major plasma proteins adsorbed to C1G1-L8-50 and C1G1-L8-100 exhibit highly similar relative abundances.

section_path: Results > The quantity of adsorbed plasma proteins affects dLNP’s efficiency to target liver hepatocytes
text: Using transgenic mice with a tdTomato (tdTom) gene flanked by loxP sites, we assessed the cell type transfected by dLNPs after delivering mRNA encoding the Cre recombinase enzyme. Immunofluorescence analysis, consistent with bioluminescence-based biodistribution analysis (Fig. 1E), showed that C1G1-L8-100 demonstrated higher liver mRNA expression (indicated by tdTomato) compared to C1G1-L8-50 (Fig. 3G). Higher magnification imaging showed that for C1G1-L8-100, most of liver mRNA expression was associated with hepatocytes (Fig. 3G, insert). Given that apolipoproteins can mediate the LNP’s targeting to hepatocytes through LDLR, we selectively analyzed the relative abundance of apolipoproteins between the sister formulations. Overall, the relative abundance of apolipoproteins was similar in both formulations (27.4% for C1G1-L8-50 and 24.3% for C1G1-L8-100) (Supplementary 3, Fig. S9A, light blue bars). Further analysis of major identified apolipoproteins (e.g., Apoa1, Apob, Apoe, Apc3, Apoa4, and Apoh) found no significant differential expression of each apolipoprotein category (Fig. 3H). However, since the amount of total protein associated with C1G1-L8-100 was twice that of C1G1-L8-50 (Fig. 3A–E), the absolute abundance of apolipoproteins was lower in C1G1-L8-50. This reduced protein abundance in C1G1-L8-50 may impair apolipoproteins’ ability to facilitate dLNP’s targeting to hepatocytes, resulting in significantly lower liver mRNA expression for C1G1-L8-50. To further confirm this hypothesis, we analyzed the protein corona composition of another sister formulation: C5G0-L12-50 and C5G0-L12-100. The total amount of plasma proteins associated with the C5G0-L12-100 was approximately twofold higher than that of the C5G0-L12-50 (Fig. 3A). Proteomics analysis found a higher relative abundance of apolipoproteins in the protein corona of C5G0-L12-100 (28.9%) over C5G0-L12-50 (19.0%), which is mostly driven by Apoa1 (21.9% versus 13.1%) (Tables S3 and S4, Supplementary 3, Fig. S9B and C).

section_path: Results > The quantity of adsorbed plasma proteins affects dLNP’s efficiency to target liver hepatocytes
text: To evaluate the impact of the protein corona on hepatocyte transfection for both formulations, we first assessed transfection efficiency in the presence or absence of 25% human serum using the Huh7.5 human hepatocyte cell line, which expresses high levels of surface LDLR. Our results demonstrated that the addition of 25% serum significantly enhanced the transfection efficiency of C1G1-L8-100 by 4.2-fold, while it reduced the efficiency of C1G1-L8-50 by 1.9-fold (Fig. 3I, left). For C1G1-L8-100, transfection efficiency was also found to be dependent on the serum concentration (Supplementary 3, Fig. S10). In contrast, when tested on another human hepatocyte cell line, SK-Hep-1 cells with low LDLR expression, the presence of 25% human serum did not significantly affect transfection efficiency (Fig. 3I, right). To further investigate the role of apolipoproteins in mediating hepatocyte transfection, we preincubated C1G1-L8-50 and C1G1-L8-100 dLNPs with recombinant human ApoE (0.25 g ApoE per g total lipid) and transfected Huh7.5 cells using escalating doses of mRNA. Overall, C1G1-L8-100 exhibited higher transfection efficiency in Huh7.5 cells than C1G1-L8-50 (Fig. 3K); more importantly, ApoE pre-incubation significantly enhanced the transfection efficiency of C1G1-L8-100 (p = 0.0007), but not that of its sister formulation, C1G1-L8-50. Taken together, these findings suggest that the enhanced hepatocyte transfection efficiency of C1G1-L8-100 is driven by its greater adsorption of plasma proteins, particularly apolipoproteins, and by an LDLR-mediated mechanism. Conversely, the reduced protein adsorption of C1G1-L8-50 corresponds with lower hepatocyte transfection efficiency and a reduced reliance on serum proteins. This in vitro study provided a mechanistic understanding of our in vivo discovery that C1G1-L8-100 showed robust mRNA expression in the liver, while C1G1-L8-50 did not (Fig. 3J).

section_path: Results > The 50% and 100% series dLNPs both induced mRNA expression in spleen but exhibited distinct preferences for myeloid cell subsets
text: Clinical applications of mRNA-based therapeutics have a large focus on immunotherapy [2,4], in which the interactions between the delivery vehicle (i.e., LNP) and the immune system are critical for both safety and efficacy. To explore how lipid grafting affects dLNP interactions with immune tissues, we compared two sister formulations, C1G1-L8-50 and C1G1-L8-100, focusing on their targeting behaviors in immune reservoirs like the spleen, blood, and bone marrow. Using transgenic mice with a tdTomato gene flanked by loxP sites (Fig. 4A), we assessed the cell types transfected by dLNPs after delivering mRNA encoding the Cre recombinase enzyme. Total spleen mRNA expression was analyzed by quantifying the percentage of tdTom + splenocytes, showing similar results for both formulations (Fig. 4B), consistent with bioluminescence data (Fig. 3J). Histological analysis revealed that tdTom expression was mainly localized in the marginal zone for C1G1-L8-50, while in C1G1-L8-100, it was distributed across the red pulp (Fig. 4C). Flow cytometry confirmed that both dLNPs were more effective at transfecting myeloid cells in the marginal zone and red pulp than T and B cells in the white pulp (Supplementary 3, Fig.S11 A–C, gating strategy is provided in the same figure). This explained that for 50% series dLNPs, it showed spleen-preferential mRNA expression due to its ability to transfect splenic myeloid cells, while it lacks the ability to transfect hepatocytes in the liver.

section_path: Results > The 50% and 100% series dLNPs both induced mRNA expression in spleen but exhibited distinct preferences for myeloid cell subsets
text: Further analysis showed that the two formulations had different preferences for myeloid cell subsets. Specifically, C1G1-L8-50 predominantly transfected granulocytes (94.9 ± 5.9%), which was 5.4-fold higher than monocytes (17.7 ± 7.9%), 8.7-fold higher than macrophages (10.9 ± 2.0%), and 37.7-fold higher than dendritic cells (2.5 ± 0.3%) (Fig. 4D, red bars; Supplementary 3, Fig. S11D). In contrast, C1G1-L8-100 was more efficient in transfecting monocytes (34.6 ± 27.3%) and dendritic cells (29.5 ± 28.8%) but less effective with granulocytes (41.6 ± 40.4%) compared to C1G1-L8-50 (Fig. 4D, blue bars; Supplementary 3, Fig. S11D), making C1G1-L8-100 less specific to granulocytes than C1G1-L8-50. Since the delivery of mRNA to splenocytes is influenced by tissue barriers that may restrict dLNP access, we next evaluated transfection in the peripheral blood, where access to leukocytes is unrestricted. In the blood, C1G1-L8-50 showed greater specificity for granulocytes (68.0 ± 17.6%), which was 21.1-fold higher than monocytes (3.2 ± 0.5%), 7.8-fold higher than macrophages (8.7 ± 5.9%), and 67.2-fold higher than dendritic cells (1.0 ± 0.2%) (Fig. 4E, red bars). In contrast, C1G1-L8-100 had higher transfection efficiency in monocytes (26.2 ± 12.9%), macrophages (23.0 ± 16.0%), and dendritic cells (4.6 ± 2.2%) but lower efficiency in granulocytes (52.1 ± 18.7%) (Fig. 4E, blue bars), making it less specific to granulocytes than C1G1-L8-50. We further performed an in vitro assay using primary bone marrow cells to validate this in vivo discovery (Supplementary 3, Fig. S14A). A heterogenous population of murine bone marrow cells was transfected with either C1G1-L8-50 or C1G1-L8-100, and the granulocyte-to-monocyte ratio was quantified in transfected cells using flow cytometry (Supplementary 3, Fig. S14C). Notably, the C1G1-L8-50 group exhibited a 3-fold higher granulocyte-to-monocyte ratio compared to C1G1-L8-100, suggesting that the 50% series formulation has higher preferential transfection towards granulocytes than the 100% series formulation (Supplementary 3, Fig. S14C).

section_path: Results > The 50% and 100% series dLNPs both induced mRNA expression in spleen but exhibited distinct preferences for myeloid cell subsets
text: When analyzing the protein corona of 50% series vs. 100% series dLNPs, we found that complement proteins and immunoglobulins, although accounting for less than 3% of the total proteins in both formulations, were uniquely associated with C1G1-L8-50 (Supplementary 3, Fig. S13). Complement proteins, such as C1s1, Mbl (Mannose-binding lectin), and C4b, were more abundant in C1G1-L8-50 (2.71%) than in C1G1-L8-100 (0.57%) (Fig. 4F, left, Supplementary 3, Fig. S9A). Collectively, this data indicated proteins associated with the complement system are more enriched in surface of C1G1-L8-50.

section_path: Results > Construct quaternary amine (QA) dendrimers for lung-specific mRNA delivery
text: Recent studies demonstrated that incorporating cationic lipids, such as DOTAP and chemically modified cationic cholesterol, into LNP formulations enables lung-selective mRNA delivery [3,11,12]. Inspired by these findings, we designed a small library of cationic dendrimers by converting internal amines into permanently charged quaternary amines (QAs), aiming to identify lung-tropic dLNP formulations. We selected seven lead dendrimers from the 100% and 50% dLNP series (Fig. 5A) and modified them with two approaches to introduce QAs: (i) partial conversion of core dendrimer amines (QAP dendrimers) (Fig. 5B, top) and (ii) full conversion of both core and terminal amines (QAF dendrimers) (Fig. 5B, bottom). Given that QA influences both toxicity and transfection efficiency, we formulated 14 QA dendrimers into dLNPs by mixing with helper lipids at 5 distinct molar ratios, creating a library of 70 QA-containing dLNPs (dLNPQA). In vitro screening identified three leading dendrimer categories: C5G0-L12-100, C4G0-UNL-100, and C1G1-L8-50 (Fig. 5C), with all QAF-based formulations proving too toxic for in vivo use. While C1G1-L8-50QAP showed limited transfection, C4G0-UNL-100QAP and C5G0-L12-100QAP were both potent and safe (Fig. 5D and E). Of note, C4G0-UNL-100QAP dLNPs were composed of dendrimer-lipid, DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG 2000 at a molar ratio of 50:10:38:2, respectively. C5G0-L12-100QAP dLNPs were composed of the same components at a molar ratio of 25:35:38:2, respectively. Bioluminescence data revealed robust lung mRNA expression from both C4G0-UNL-100QAP and C5G0-L12-100QAP compared to their unmodified versions (Fig. 5D, Supplementary 3, Fig. S15). Notably, C5G0-L12-100QAP demonstrated strong lung-preferential expression, with 91.7 ± 7.3% of mRNA expression in the lung, significantly higher than its unmodified counterpart (5.5 ± 4.2%) (Fig. 5E). Further validation in transgenic tdTomato reporter mice confirmed the lung-specific expression of C5G0-L12-100QAP (Fig. 5F).

section_path: Results > dLNPQA target lung epithelial cells through a mechanism independent of total protein abundance
text: To investigate the underlying mechanism of lung-specific delivery in dLNPQA, we first compared their zeta potential with their sister formulations in the 100% series dLNP and found that QA modification did not make the dLNP surface cationic, potentially due to the presence of PEG on the dLNPQA surface (C4G0-UNL-100: −1.80 ± 0.20 mV, C4G0-UNL-100QAP: 0.13 ± 0.59 mV; C5G0-L12-100: −1.63 ± 0.95 mV, C5G0-L12-100QAP: 0.13 ± 0.23 mV). In addition, the QA modification did not significantly increase the size of dLNPs (C4G0-UNL-100: 240.9 ± 14.6 nm, C4G0-UNL-100QAP: 150.5 ± 1.28 nm; C5G0-L12-100: 142.9 ± 1.9 nm, C5G0-L12-100QAP: 148.1 ± 3.3 nm). To further ensure the lungspecificity of dLNPQA was not caused by their aggregation and trapping in lung capillaries, we evaluated the stability of C5G0-L12-100QAP. C5G0-L12-100QAP maintained excellent stability in PBS (Supplementary 3, Fig. S16A). In the presence of plasma, the size distribution of C5G0-L12-100QAP became more heterogenous over the 3-h window. This level of stability was similar to the liver-targeting sister formulation C5G0-L12-100 (Supplementary 3, Fig. S16B). No significant population with size larger than 300 nm was observed. Collectively, this evidence demonstrated that the lung-specificity of dLNPQA was not due to their aggregation in the blood.

section_path: Results > dLNPQA target lung epithelial cells through a mechanism independent of total protein abundance
text: To assess the role of protein corona in mediating the lung-specificity of dLNPQA, we first quantified the plasma protein corona abundance. Interestingly, protein quantification showed no difference in the total plasma protein abundance between C5G0-L12-100 and C5G0-L12-100QAP (Fig. 5G). The PRODAN assay revealed that the hydrophobicity of C5G0-L12-100QAP was approximately 2-fold lower than its 100% series counterparts (Supplementary 3, Fig. S17A). However, the weaker hydrophobic interactions in the 100QA series dLNPs may be compensated by stronger electrostatic interactions due to the cationic QA dendrimers. Although the TNS assay did not successfully determine the apparent pKa of C5G0-L12-100QAP, the TNS curve for the 100QA series showed a gap at higher pH, specifically between pH 9 and 12 (Supplementary 3, Fig. S17B). This gap suggests residual interactions between TNS salts and C5G0-L12-100QAP, likely due to the permanently cationic nature of the QA dendrimers. This was not observed for the 100% series formulations, which lack QA dendrimers. A significant drop in TNS fluorescence was observed at pH above 12, indicating reduced electrostatic interactions due to the neutralization of the cationic QAs. Overall, our results indicated that the cationic properties of 100QA series dLNPs enhance their binding to plasma proteins through electrostatic interactions, leading to similar protein adsorption levels.

section_path: Results > dLNPQA target lung epithelial cells through a mechanism independent of total protein abundance
text: SDS-PAGE analysis revealed distinct plasma protein components between C5G0-L12-100 and C5G0-L12-100QAP. Specifically, proteins at 70 kDa, just above 150 kDa, and 25 kDa were enriched in C5G0-L12-100QAP (Fig. 5H, green boxes), while proteins at 20 kDa and between 85 and 100 kDa were enriched in C5G0-L12-100 (Fig. 5H, blue boxes). Proteomic analysis showed that ApoE and ApoB, which are known to mediate liver-preferential expression in LNPs [6,11,34] are more enriched in the C5G0-L12-100 (Fig. 5I). In contrast, only Vtn was uniquely enriched in C5G0-L12-100QAP (Fig. 5I). Vtn has been identified in another study to be associated with lung-selective LNP delivery, as it facilitates binding to its receptor, αvβ3 integrin, highly expressed in the pulmonary endothelium [11]. To determine whether lung epithelial cells were responsible for the lung-targeting of dLNPQA, we conducted an immunofluorescent study based on the lung tissue harvested from the C5G0-L12-100QAP injected Ai14 mice (Fig. 5J). Our results showed high levels of co-localization between tdTomato expression and anti-CD324 antibody, which labels epithelial cells through E-cadherin, indicating lung epithelial cells were responsible for lung-specificity of C5G0-L12-100QAP. We further validated this hypothesis in vitro using a human lung cancer epithelial cell line NCI–H292 that expresses αvβ3 integrin [46]. Here, we preincubated C5G0-L12-100 and C5G0-L12-100QAP formulations encapsulating luciferase mRNA with increasing amounts of Vtn. Interestingly, Vtn enhanced functional mRNA delivery of both sister formulations, suggesting that both formulations can efficiently bind Vtn and enter αvβ3-expressing cells (Fig. 5K). However, when these formulations were incubated with human serum, only the transfection of C5G0-L12-100QAP was significantly enhanced (Fig. 5L). This suggests that in the presence of an ensemble of proteins, C5G0-L12-100 preferentially binds other constituents, limiting its transfection in lung epithelial cells. These findings support that the extrahepatic delivery of 100QA series dLNPs is not driven by reduced protein adsorption, but rather by signature proteins like Vtn that are abundantly adsorbed to C5G0-L12-100QAP, contributing to its lung-selectivity.

section_path: Discussion
text: In this study, we utilized PAMAM dendrimers as modular building blocks to construct a library of dLNPs with varying structural properties. A systematic structure-function analysis revealed that the percentage of lipid grafting significantly influenced the in vivo tissue-specific delivery of mRNA through a novel mechanism driven primarily by dLNP hydrophobicity. This finding expands current knowledge, which focuses on elucidating the mechanism of LNP’s tissue-specific delivery from the perspective of apparent pKa [11]. Specifically, LNPs with a low apparent pKa (2 to 6) and higher apparent pKa (>9) have been shown to mediate efficient nucleic acid delivery to the spleen [3,11–13,20,47]. However, a recent study reported a weak correlation between apparent pKa and splenic mRNA expression [15]. Emerging evidence suggests that the lipid tail structures also have a significant impact on extrahepatic RNA delivery. For example, dendron-like ionizable lipids with multi-armed tails [21], ionizable lipids with branched biodegradable tails [14,23], and lipids with short tails [17,18,20] have all been shown to increase mRNA delivery to the spleen or lung. Collectively, these findings indicate that apparent pKa may not be the sole determinant of LNP tissue-specific delivery.

section_path: Discussion
text: We found that reducing the lipid grafting percentage on the dendrimer surface enabled extrahepatic delivery of dLNPs, highlighting the impact of lipid tail structures on LNP biodistribution. We hypothesized that dLNP cell and tissue tropism is mediated by the hydrophobicity of LNPs. Previous studies have shown the importance of hydrophobicity in determining protein adsorption for polymeric and inorganic nanoparticles [26–28]. However, due to the lack of a method to characterize LNP hydrophobicity, its impact on LNPs’ in vivo behavior has remained unclear. Early studies showed that the lipid structure can affect the packing density of liposomal membranes, which has significant impact on liposome stability and half-life in plasma due to the interactions with apolipoproteins and HDLs [48,49]. Here, we extended the study to the LNP system. Specifically, we developed a fluorescent probe-based assay to quantify dLNP surface hydrophobicity. This assay revealed that lower lipid grafting percentage (50% series) significantly reduced hydrophobicity in both dLNPs and conventional LNPs based on clinically approved ionizable lipids. Notably, this reduced surface hydrophobicity caused the 50% series dLNPs to be more unstable than the 100% series in the plasma. This phenomenon was also observed in formulations based on clinical ionizable lipids SM-102 and ALC-0315 (Fig. 3B, Supplementary 3, Fig. S5B–D). SM-102 LNPs exhibited lower surface hydrophobicity (Fig. 2L), reduced total plasma protein adsorption (Supplementary 3, Fig. S7), and increased spleen-preferential mRNA expression compared to ALC-0315 LNPs (Fig. 2K). These findings collectively indicated that the lower surface hydrophobicity makes LNPs less stable in the plasma, leading to reduced adsorption of plasma proteins on the LNP surface, and also suggesting that the relationship among LNP surface hydrophobicity, protein adsorption, and tissue tropism identified in our dLNP system may extend to conventional LNP platforms. Previous studies have shown that LNPs and liposomes with reduced PEG surface coverage exhibit decreased plasma stability and increased uptake by the Mononuclear Phagocyte System (MPS), resulting in accelerated systemic clearance and enhanced splenic accumulation [50,51]. In our study, we demonstrate that altering lipid grafting percentage and surface hydrophobicity similarly modulates the stability of dLNPs. Reduced particle stability was associated with reduced liver mRNA expression while maintaining robust splenic mRNA expression, likely due to interactions with phagocytic cells. Future studies establishing a direct link between decreased LNP stability, accelerated systemic clearance, and reduced liver accumulation will be necessary to further validate this proposed mechanism. Similarly, the 100QA series dLNPs exhibited significantly lower surface hydrophobicity compared to their 100% series counterparts. However, unlike the 50% series, where reduced surface hydrophobicity was due to lower lipid grafting percentage, the 100QA series’ reduced surface hydrophobicity was driven by the permanently cationic dendrimer cores. This demonstrates that both the ionizable head and lipid tail structures influence LNP surface hydrophobicity.

section_path: Discussion
text: By characterizing the plasma proteins associated with dLNPs, we identified a hydrophobicity-driven mechanism that mediates their extrahepatic delivery. Current theory suggests that the spleen tropism of LNPs is primarily driven by β2-GPI, a plasma protein highly enriched in the protein corona of LNPs with a low apparent pKa [11]. However, in our system, the spleen-targeting dLNPs had a higher apparent pKa range (7.5 to 8.4). Additionally, the relative abundance of key plasma proteins (Apoa1, Vtn, and Alb) associated with both the 50% (spleen tropism) and 100% (liver tropism) series dLNPs did not differ significantly. This suggests that spleen-preferential expression in the 50% series dLNPs is not driven by a specific plasma protein. Instead, it is likely caused by reduced total protein adsorption in the less hydrophobic 50% series formulation. This reduction in protein adsorption decreased the number of apolipoproteins bound to the 50% series dLNPs, resulting in significantly reduced transfection towards hepatocytes compared to the 100% series dLNPs. As a result, the 50% series dLNP showed a strong spleen specific mRNA expression through targeting splenic myeloid cells. Further studies are needed to confirm this hypothesis by comparing the affinity of apolipoproteins for the 50% and 100% series dLNPs. The extrahepatic delivery of 100QA series dLNPs was not driven by total protein abundance. Although these dLNPs had significantly lower surface hydrophobicity than the 100% series, their cationic surface properties likely facilitated interactions with different plasma proteins. Consequently, the protein corona composition differed significantly between C5G0-L12-100 and C5G0-L12-100QAP (Tables S3 and S5). We show that lung-selective delivery of C5G0-L12-100QAP was mediated by targeting epithelial cells, which is mediated by one or more endogenous proteins.

section_path: Discussion
text: The topography and surface chemistry of nanoparticles are critical features in triggering complement recognition [52]. Here, we observed a higher relative abundance of complement proteins and immunoglobulins associated with the 50% series dLNPs. It is possible that the reduced lipid grafting in the 50% series formulations led to faster shedding of PEG, exposing the ionizable head groups on the dendrimer surface and enabling more efficient binding of complement proteins (e.g., C1q, Mbl, C3b) and immunoglobulins (e.g., IgM) through recognition of these specific nanoparticle surface chemistries [53]. However, it should be noted that the plasma used in our study contains K2 EDTA as an anti-coagulant, which can impair the cascade of complement activation. Although it is unknown whether the presence of K2 EDTA affects the binding of complement protein with dLNPs, we acknowledge that study based on complement-active plasma is required to further validate this observation. Since myeloid cells express high levels of complement protein receptors, which play a role in nanoparticle phagocytosis [53], further mechanistic studies should focus on connecting the complement protein enrichment in C1G1-L8-50 to their high specificity towards granulocytic myeloid cells.

section_path: Discussion
text: While the lead dLNPQA formulations did not show observable acute adverse effects in this study, a comprehensive preclinical safety evaluation will be necessary to fully characterize the safety profile of cationic dLNP formulations. Such studies should include serum biochemistry, cytokine profiling, hematologic and coagulation analyses, and histopathology, given that cationic lipids have been associated with multiple toxicity mechanisms including fibrinogen-mediated thrombosis, complement activation, and hemolysis. Similarly, although our two-dose Ai14 reporter studies did not reveal a substantial shift in tissue tropism, dedicated evaluation of accelerated blood clearance following repeated dosing will be an important future direction for translational development of these formulations.

section_path: Discussion
text: In summary, the observed differences in cell and tissue specificity among our dLNP formulations are driven by variations in dendrimer lipid grafting percentage, which modulates LNP surface hydrophobicity and, in turn, the quantity and composition of adsorbed plasma proteins. Although our results demonstrate a strong correlation among dendrimer lipid grafting percentage, dLNP surface hydrophobicity, and tissuespecific mRNA delivery, future studies will be necessary to establish a direct causal relationship between LNP hydrophobicity and cell and tissue tropism. Such efforts could include systematically varying LNP surface hydrophobicity while holding other physicochemical parameters constant to isolate its contribution to in vivo biodistribution.

section_path: Conclusions
text: In summary, this study extends the current framework of LNP-mediated nucleic acid delivery by demonstrating that the structure of lipid tails can drive extrahepatic delivery through modulating LNP surface hydrophobicity. While our findings were primarily derived from dendrimer-based systems, we observed consistent hydrophobicity-driven trends in LNPs formulated with clinically approved ionizable lipids SM-102 and ALC-0315 (Fig. 2J–L), supporting the broader applicability of this mechanism across LNP platforms. Further investigations across additional lipid platforms will be valuable to fully establish the generalizability of this principle. Notably, although 50% series dLNPs exhibited superior transfection efficiency compared to their 100% series counterparts in vitro in the absence of serum proteins, their overall in vivo transfection potency was markedly lower (Supplementary 3, Figs. S1 and S2). Additionally, while in vitro cytotoxicity screening was performed to select lead formulations with high relative cell viability prior to in vivo studies, and no acute toxicity was observed in animals at the administered dose, a comprehensive biosafety evaluation including assessment of liver and kidney function and systemic inflammatory responses was not conducted. As the primary focus of this work was to elucidate the mechanistic role of surface hydrophobicity in modulating the nano-bio interface and tissue-selective delivery, detailed toxicological characterization of the dLNP platform remains an important direction for future investigation. Given that reducing LNP surface hydrophobicity can reduce the total abundance of adsorbed proteins and enable extrahepatic delivery while increasing the complement protein adsorption, future efforts can focus on optimizing dendrimer chemistry to reduce complement recognition while maintaining the low surface hydrophobicity of 50% series dLNPs to enable more efficient extrahepatic delivery.
