section_path: Materials and methods > Synthesis of generation 1 (G1) and generation 2 (G2) dendrimers
text: Dendrimers derived from Core #1 (C1) were commercially available and used without further modification or purification. Dendrimer synthesis procedures were adapted from previously published protocols [54]. G1 dendrimers were synthesized using a two-step reaction process involving Michael addition and amidation. Initially, initiator cores were individually reacted with an excess of methyl acrylate in anhydrous methanol. The reactions were initiated on ice and gradually brought to room temperature, where they proceeded for 24 h. The resulting Michael addition products were purified by methanol co-evaporation using a rotary evaporator (BUCHI, Rotavapor® R-100). In the second step, amidation was carried out by reacting the purified intermediates separately with an excess of ethylenediamine in anhydrous methanol. These reactions were also initiated on ice and then allowed to proceed at room temperature for 96 h. The final G1 dendrimers were purified using a 9:1 toluene-to-methanol ratio, followed by methanol co-evaporation via rotary evaporation. The purity and chemical structure of the final G1 dendrimers were confirmed by proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy (Bruker, 600 MHz) in methanol-d4 (CD3OD) prior to further use. All NMR spectra were analyzed using MestReNova version 14.2.1 (Mestrelab Research, Spain), and chemical shifts are reported in parts per million (ppm). G2 dendrimers were synthesized using the same two-step reaction scheme as G1 dendrimers, with G1 dendrimers serving as the starting material in place of initiator cores. The purity and chemical structure of the final G2 dendrimers were also confirmed by 1H NMR in CD3OD prior to further use.

section_path: Materials and methods > Synthesis of dendrimer-based ionizable lipids (dILs)
text: Dendrimer-based ionizable lipids (dILs) were synthesized according to previously published protocols with modifications [55]. G0 (Core), G1, and G2 dendrimers were reacted with epoxides (long-chain alkyl epoxides or glycidyl ethers) of varying chain lengths (8-carbon and 12-carbon) and structural types (branched and unsaturated). When the stoichiometric amount of epoxide equaled the total number of terminal amine reactive sites within the dendrimer (two sites per primary amine), the resulting products were designated as 100-series dILs. Conversely, when the stoichiometric amount of epoxide was set at half the total number of terminal amine reactive sites, the products were classified as 50-series dILs. The reactions were conducted in 20-mL amber vials containing 200-proof anhydrous ethanol as the solvent and heated at 90 °C for 96 h. Crude products were initially concentrated using a rotary evaporator to remove residual ethanol and subsequently redissolved in dichloromethane (DCM) for further purification. For in vitro transfection efficiency and cell viability screening, the crude dILs were purified using preparative thin-layer chromatography (Prep TLC) on silica gel plates (1000 μm thickness, Miles Scientific) with an 88:11:1 DCM/MeOH/Et3N (v/v/v) solvent system. For dILs selected for in vivo animal studies (herein referred to as lead dILs), purification was performed via silica gel column chromatography (high-purity grade, pore size 60 Å, Supelco) using a gradient elution from 98:1:1 to 80:19:1 DCM/MeOH/Et3N (v/v/v). The purity and identity of lead dIL fractions were confirmed by silica gel thin-layer chromatography (Supelco) with the 88:11:1 DCM/MeOH/Et3N solvent system, wherein each dIL series appeared as a distinct band on the TLC plates. Desired fractions were pooled, and concentrated by rotary evaporation, and the final products were lyophilized (Labconco) for 72 h. The chemical structures of the purified lead dILs were characterized by 1H NMR (Bruker, 600 MHz) and 13C NMR (Bruker, 151 MHz) in chloroform-d (CDCl3, Sigma-Aldrich). The purity profile of lead dILs was further evaluated using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Vanquish high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system equipped with a binary pump, dual UV detector, autosampler, and the Chromeleon™ Chromatography Data System (CDS). Chromatograms were recorded simultaneously at 210 nm and 250 nm. The mobile phase consisted of freshly prepared, filtered, and degassed HPLC-grade water (H2O) and acetonitrile (ACN). Separation was performed on a Supelco Discovery® C8 column (5 μm particle size, 25 cm length, 4.6 mm internal diameter) under an isocratic method with 50% H2O and 50% ACN for 30 min at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. Electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS, Advion expression CMS or Waters Xevo TQ-S micro) was also performed to confirm that the desired product was obtained.

section_path: Materials and methods > Synthesis of dILs with partial quaternary amine modification
text: Select dILs purified via column chromatography were subjected to partial quaternization by reacting with an excess of CH3I in THF at 40 °C for 72 h. Following the reaction, THF and unreacted CH3I were removed using a rotary evaporator. The crude products were washed three times with hexane and dried under vacuum. The final products were lyophilized for 72 h. The structures of quaternary amine-modified dILs selected for animal studies were confirmed by 1H, 13C, DEPTQ-135, and HSQC NMRs prior to use. HPLC and ESI-MS were also performed as final confirmation of the desired product.

section_path: Materials and methods > Synthesis of dILs with full quaternary amine modification
text: The same purified dILs from above were reacted with an excess of CH3I (as both reactant and solvent) at room temperature for 72 h to obtain fully quaternary amine-modified dILs. Unreacted CH3I was removed under vacuum, and the crude products were washed three times with hexane before being dried under vacuum. The final products were lyophilized for 72 h, and their structures were confirmed using 1H, 13C, DEPTQ-135, and HSQC NMRs prior to use.

section_path: Materials and methods > Nanoparticle preparation
text: Unless otherwise stated, all lipids were dissolved in ethanol at defined molar ratios, while mRNAs (FLuc or Cre) were diluted in 10 mM citrate buffer (pH 4.5). The two phases were rapidly mixed at a volume ratio of 3:1 (mRNA to lipids, v/v), and a mass ratio of 40:1 (total lipids to mRNA, w/w), followed by equilibration at room temperature for 10 min prior to utilization. For dLNPs, dendrimer-based lipids (dILs), DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG 2000 were dissolved in ethanol at a molar ratio of 50:10:38:2. For quaternary amine-modified dendrimer-based lipid nanoparticles (dLNPQA), quaternary amine-modified dILs were formulated with DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG 2000 at five distinct molar ratios: 5:55:38:2 (Ratio 1), 10:50:38:2 (Ratio 2), 15:45:38:2 (Ratio 3), 20:40:38:2 (Ratio 4), and 25:35:38:2 (Ratio 5). SM-102, DLin-MC3-DMA, and jetMESSENGER® were prepared according to the manufacturers’ protocols, while C12-200 was formulated following a previously published method [56]. For the DOTAP liposome formulation, the cationic lipid DOTAP was combined with cholesterol and DMG-PEG 2000 at a molar ratio of 49.5:49.5:1. For ALC-0315 LNP formulation, the ionizable lipid ALC-0315 was dissolved in ethanol with DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG 2000 at a molar ratio 50:10:38.5:1.5.

section_path: Materials and methods > Characterization of dLNPs > Physicochemical properties:
text: The hydrodynamic diameter, polydispersity index (PDI), and zeta (ζ) potential were measured using dynamic light scattering (Anton Paar, Litesizer DLS 500) at 25 ° C. dLNPs encapsulating 1 μg of mRNA were prepared as previously described and diluted to 1 mL with 1× PBS to achieve a final lipid concentration of 40 μg/mL. Hydrodynamic diameter and PDI were measured using disposable cuvettes (Sarstedt), while ζ potential was measured using omega cuvettes (Anton Paar). To further characterize particle size distribution and concentration, nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) was performed using the ZetaView® QUATT (Particle Metrix). For NTA measurements, dLNPs encapsulating 1 μg of mRNA were prepared as previously described, diluted 10,000-fold in 1× PBS, and injected into the instrument for analysis.

section_path: Materials and methods > Characterization of dLNPs > Encapsulation efficiency:
text: The mRNA encapsulation efficiency of each dLNP formulation was quantified using the Invitrogen™ Quant-iT™ RiboGreen Reagent and RNA Assay Kit, following the manufacturer’s protocol.

section_path: Materials and methods > Characterization of dLNPs > Cryo-electron microscopy (Cryo-EM):
text: Cryo-electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) imaging was conducted at the Structural Biology Cryo-Electron Microscopy Core, Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation & Technology (Jupiter, FL). A 3 μL aliquot of purified and concentrated dLNPs in PBS was applied onto glow-discharged copper grids with 2 μm holes (C-Flat CF2/2 400 mesh, Electron Microscopy Sciences, Hatfield, PA). The grids were immediately vitrified (rapid freezing) using a Mark IV Vitrobot (FEI Co., Hillsboro, OR) under 95% humidity in the sample chamber. Imaging was performed using a JEOL Cryo ARM™ 300 (JEOL USA, Inc., Peabody, MA). The transmission electron microscope was operated at 300 kV, and data were captured using a Gatan K3 detector with an Omega filter set to 20 eV. Regions of interest were selected for imaging using SerialEM. dLNPs were imaged at magnifications of 8,000× and 60,000×, with a total electron dose of 50 e−/Å2 and 50 frames for the high-magnification movies. Movie frames were aligned, and contrast transfer function (CTF) estimation was performed using Patch Motion Correction and Patch CTF Estimation in CryoSPARC (Toronto, Canada).

section_path: Materials and methods > Characterization of dLNPs > Apparent pKa:
text: The apparent pKa of dLNP formulations was determined using the TNS fluorescence assay. Briefly, a series of pH buffers (ranging from 2.5 to 12) were prepared with 150 mM sodium chloride and 20 mM citrate, phosphate, or borate buffers. A 0.6 mM TNS stock solution was freshly prepared in deionized water. For the assay, 188 μL of the respective pH buffer, 12 μL of dLNP, and 2 μL of TNS were combined in the wells of black-bottom 96-well plate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, M33089). After a 10-min incubation at room temperature under continuous orbital shaking, fluorescence intensity was measured using a plate reader (Molecular Devices, SpectraMax iD3) at an excitation wavelength (λEx) of 325 nm and an emission wavelength (λEm) of 447 nm. The fluorescence data were normalized to the value at the lowest pH, and a sigmoidal curve fit was applied to the normalized data. The apparent pKa was defined as the pH corresponding to half-maximal (0.5) fluorescence intensity.

section_path: Materials and methods > Characterization of dLNPs > Surface hydrophobicity characterization:
text: The surface hydrophobicity of dLNPs was evaluated using a modified PRODAN fluorescence assay. A 1 mM PRODAN stock solution was freshly prepared in methanol before each experiment. Two complementary assay formats were employed. In the first method, dLNPs were incubated with the previously described series of pH buffers. Specifically, 188 μL of the respective buffer, 12 μL of dLNP, and 1 μL of PRODAN were dispensed into black-bottom 96-well plates. Following a 10-min incubation at room temperature, fluorescence was measured using a plate reader (Molecular Devices, SpectraMax iD3 or Agilent BioTek Cytation) at an excitation wavelength (λEx) of 365 nm and an emission wavelength (λEm) of 435 nm. The dLNP surface hydrophobicity was quantified as the maximum fluorescence intensity at the plateau phase. In the second method, dLNPs were serially diluted in 188 μL of PBS buffer (pH 7.4) and incubated for 10 min. Subsequently, 1 μL of PRODAN was added, and fluorescence was measured using a plate reader (Agilent BioTek Cytation 1). The hydrophobicity index (S0) was calculated as the initial slope obtained from linear regression analysis. Detailed characterization data for each formation are provided in Fig. 2E–G and Supplementary 3, Fig. S3.

section_path: Materials and methods > Stability of dLNPs in plasma
text: A subset of lead dLNP formulations (C1G1-L8-50, C1G1-L8-100, C5G0-L12-100, and C5G0-L12-100QA), together with two clinically approved LNPs (SM-102 and ALC-0315), were prepared as described above with the addition of 0.5% (molar ratio) fluorescent helper lipid TMR-PC (Avanti Polar Lipids) and concentrated to 1 mg/mL. Equal volumes of the concentrated LNPs and mouse plasma (Innovative Research) were incubated for 180 min. Particle size distributions were then measured using fluorescent NTA (ZetaView QUATT) with a 520 nm excitation laser and a 550 nm emission filter.

section_path: Materials and methods > Isolation, characterization, and proteomic analysis of dLNP protein corona > Isolation of plasma proteins adsorbed to dLNPs:
text: Plasma proteins adsorbed to the surface of dLNPs were isolated following a published protocol [11]. Briefly, dLNPs were prepared as previously described and concentrated to a final lipid concentration of 1 mg/mL. The concentrated dLNPs were then incubated with an equal volume of mouse plasma (C57BL6 plasma supplemented with anticoagulant K2 EDTA, Innovative Research) at 37 °C for 15 min. The dLNP/plasma mixture was layered onto a 0.7 M sucrose cushion at an equal volume and centrifuged at 15, 300 × g for 1 h at 4 °C. The resulting pellet was washed three times with cold 1× PBS, with each wash followed by centrifugation at 15,300 × g for 5 min. After the final wash, the pellet was resuspended in 1× PBS and quantified using the Pierce™ Bradford Protein Assay Kit following the manufacturer’s protocol. The samples were then submitted to the University of Florida Department of Chemistry Mass Spectrometry Research and Education Center for mass spectrometry and proteomics analysis.

section_path: Materials and methods > Isolation, characterization, and proteomic analysis of dLNP protein corona > SDS-PAGE characterization of plasma proteins:
text: A total of 8 μg of plasma proteins isolated from the dLNP surface were loaded onto an Invitrogen™ NuPAGE™ 4-12% Bis-Tris gel and electrophoresed at 200 V for 50 min. The gel was stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue for 1 h, then destained in deionized (DI) water overnight. Imaging was performed using the Bio-Rad ChemiDoc Imaging System.

section_path: Materials and methods > Isolation, characterization, and proteomic analysis of dLNP protein corona > Preparation of plasma proteins for mass spectrometry:
text: Proteins were prepared for digestion using the EasyPep™ MS Sample Prep Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Total protein concentration was quantified using an Invitrogen™ Qubit™ 3 Fluorometer, and an appropriate volume of each sample was adjusted to contain 20 μg of total protein for digestion. Proteolytic digestion was carried out using the sequencing-grade Trypsin/Lys-C Rapid Digestion Kit (Promega, Madison, WI) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Three times the sample volume of rapid digestion buffer (provided with the kit) was added to each sample. Prior to enzymatic digestion, samples were incubated at 56 °C for 30 min with 1 μL of dithiothreitol (DTT) solution (0.1 M in 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate), followed by alkylation with 0.54 μL of 55 mM iodoacetamide in 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate and incubation at room temperature in the dark for 30 min. Trypsin/Lys-C was freshly prepared at 1 μg/μL in rapid digestion buffer, and 1 μL of enzyme solution was added to each sample. Digestion was carried out at 70 ° C for 1 h and terminated by the addition of 0.5% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis was performed immediately to ensure high-quality tryptic peptides with minimal non-specific cleavage.

section_path: Materials and methods > Isolation, characterization, and proteomic analysis of dLNP protein corona > Mass spectrometry:
text: Nano-liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (Nano-LC/MS/MS) was performed using a Thermo Scientific Q Exactive HF Orbitrap mass spectrometer equipped with an EASY-Spray nanospray source (Thermo Scientific) operated in positive ion mode. The liquid chromatography (LC) system consisted of an UltiMate™ 3000 RSLCnano system (Thermo Scientific). Mobile phase A comprised water with 0.1% formic acid, while mobile phase B consisted of acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid. For the loading pump, mobile phase A contained water with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid. A 5 μL aliquot of the sample was injected onto a Thermo Scientific μPAC™ C18 trapping column (C18, 5 μm pillar diameter, 10 mm length, 2.5 μm inter-pillar distance) at a flow rate of 10 μL/min. The sample was retained for 3 min and washed with 1% mobile phase B to desalt and concentrate the peptides. The injector port was then switched to the injection mode, transferring the peptides from the trap to the analytical column. Chromatographic separation was performed using a Thermo Scientific 110 cm μPAC™ column (C18, 5 μm pillar diameter, 110 cm length, 2.5 μm inter-pillar distance) maintained at 40 °C. The initial flow rate was set at 750 nL/min for 15 min, after which it was reduced to 250 nL/min. Peptides were eluted directly into the Q Exactive HF Orbitrap mass spectrometer using a gradient of 1% to 20% mobile phase B over 100 min, followed by an increase to 45% B over the next 20 min, with a total run time of 150 min. Mass spectrometry (MS/MS) data acquisition followed standard conditions established in the laboratory. The EASY-Spray source operated at a spray voltage of 1.5 kV and a capillary temperature of 200 °C. The scan sequence was based on the TopTen™ method, where a full MS scan was acquired across a mass range of 375–1575 Da at a resolution of 60,000, followed by MS/MS scans at a resolution of 15,000 to generate product ion spectra for amino acid sequence determination. The fifteen most abundant precursor ions in each spectrum were selected for fragmentation. The automatic gain control (AGC) target was set to 3 × 106 ions for full scans and 2 × 105 ions for MS/MS mode. The maximum ion injection time was set to 50 ms for full scans and 55 ms for MS/MS mode, with a microscan number of 1 for both modes. Higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) fragmentation was applied with a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 28 and a stepped NCE, using an isolation window of 4 m/z. Singly charged ions were excluded from MS/MS analysis, and dynamic exclusion was enabled with a repeat count of 1 within a 15-s window, also excluding isotopic peaks. A siloxane background peak at 445.12003 m/z was used as an internal lock mass. To ensure system integrity and performance, a HeLa protein digest standard was analyzed. If the number of identified proteins from the HeLa standard fell below 3,200, the instrument underwent cleaning, and new columns were installed.

section_path: Materials and methods > Isolation, characterization, and proteomic analysis of dLNP protein corona > Mass spectrometry, proteomics, bioinformatics, and statistical analysis:
text: All MS/MS spectra were analyzed using PEAKS 12.5 (Bioinformatics Solutions). Protein identification was performed against the Mus musculus database (sp_incl_isoforms, TaxID = 10090_and_subtaxonomies, v2024-10-02) and a universal protein contaminant database [57], assuming trypsin as the digestion enzyme. Database searches were conducted with a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.020 Da and a precursor ion tolerance of 10.0 ppm. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was set as a fixed modification, while methionine oxidation was specified as a variable modification. Precursor ion intensity-based label-free quantification was performed using PEAKS 12.5. The three experimental groups (C1G1-L8-50 & C1G1-L8-100, C5G0-L12-50 & C5G0-L12-100, and C5G0-L12-100 & C5G0-L12-100QAP) were compared using a non-nested study factor. Normalization was performed across all detected peptides. Protein abundances were calculated using summed abundances, where protein abundance was derived by summing the sample abundances of the associated peptide groups. Statistical analysis was conducted using Fisher’s exact test (pairwise ratio-based), incorporating low-intensity resampling value imputation. Adjusted p-values were calculated using the Benjamini-Hochberg method to control the false discovery rate.

section_path: Materials and methods > Cell culture
text: RAW 264.7 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 1% penicillin-streptomycin, 1% non-essential amino acids, 1% GlutaMax, and 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS). NCI–H292 cells were a generous gift from L. Wu (UF Medicine) and cultured in high glucose DMEM (Corning) supplemented with 1% penicillin-streptomycin and 10% FBS. Huh7.5 and SK-Hep-1 cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) supplemented with 1% penicillin-streptomycin and 10% FBS. Huh7.5 cells were a generous gift from N. Khodayari (UF Medicine) and SK-Hep-1 cells were a generous gift from T. Schmittgen (UF Pharmacy). Cells were grown in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO2. All reagents were purchased through Fisher Scientific.

section_path: Materials and methods > In vitro transfection efficiency and cell viability assays
text: RAW 264.7 cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a cell density of 40,000 cells per well in the complete media two days prior to transfection. Before transfection, the complete medium (DMEM supplied with 10% FBS) was replaced with 100 μL basal medium (DMEM without FBS). The dLNPs prepared were pipetted into DMEM medium at 0.2 μg mRNA/well. A 3-h incubation was followed to allow sufficient dLNP uptake. Cells were then washed with DMEM, and 200 μL complete medium was added to each well. A 24-h incubation was followed to allow sufficient mRNA expression. When characterizing luciferase as the reporter, cells were incubated for 10 min in 100 μL luciferin assay solution (150 μg/mL concentration, PerkinElmer) and the bioluminescence was measured by luminometer.

section_path: Materials and methods > In vitro transfection efficiency and cell viability assays
text: To evaluate the toxicity of dLNPs, dLNP-containing media was aspirated, and cells were incubated for 3 h in CellTiter Blue reagent (Promega). The fluorescence signal was measured via a plate reader and was then converted to percent cell viability. Cells being cultured in basal media for 3 h but did not receive dLNPs treatment were used as the negative control (100% viability). Cells that were exposed to 1 μL of TritonX-100 treatment for 3 h were used as the positive control (0% viability).

section_path: Materials and methods > In vitro transfection efficiency and cell viability assays
text: Huh7.5, SK-Hep-1, and NCI–H292 cells were transfected following a similar method, where 25% pooled human complement-preserved serum (Innovative Research, ICSER10ML) was used instead of FBS.

section_path: Materials and methods > In vitro transfection efficiency and cell viability assays
text: For the single-protein incubation experiments, Huh7.5 cells were transfected using dLNPs prepared with or without pre-incubation with ApoE (Human ApoE4 Recombinant Protein, PeproTech) at escalating mRNA doses of 0.025, 0.05, and 0.06 μg. After formulation, dLNPs were incubated with 0.25 g ApoE per g total lipid for 15 min at 37 °C. NCI–H292 cells were transfected using dLNPs prepared with and without incubation with Vtn (Gibco™ Vitronectin Recombinant Human Protein, Truncated). After formulation, dLNPs containing 0.1 μg mRNA were incubated with 0.25, 0.5, or 1.0 g vitronectin per g total lipid for 15 min at 37 °C.

section_path: Materials and methods > Machine learning analysis
text: This study developed multi-class deep neural network (DNN) models to identify key determinants on the transfection efficiency and cell viability for dLNPs. In brief, this study curated a database containing 131 data records on physicochemical properties, transfection efficiency, and cell viability of different dLNPs, as described above. The inputting features included dendrimer structural properties, such as lipid, core, generation, primary amine number, secondary amine number, tertiary amine number, lipid tail number, Lipid to dendrimer ratio (Mw/Mw), core structure, lipid structure, dendrimer molecular weight, lipid grafting percentage, and dLNP physicochemical properties, including dLNP size, PDI, zeta potential, and encapsulation efficiency. The model output prediction included transfection efficiency and cell viability. More details on the values of input variables, parameters on the architecture of the DNN model, model training and validation processes, model evaluation metrics, and feature importance analysis using the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) methods, please refer to Supplementary 2.

section_path: Materials and methods > Animals
text: All animal studies were approved by the University of Florida Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and were consistent with local, state, and federal regulations, as applicable. All mice used in our experiments were obtained from Jackson Laboratory. Mice were treated according to the timelines and dosing regimens described in the corresponding figures.

section_path: Materials and methods > Ex vivo imaging > Bioluminescence imaging:
text: B6(Cg)-Tyrc–2J/J mice (Jackson Laboratories, 20-25 g) were intravenously injected with dLNPs (~100 μL for female and ~125 μL for male) via the tail vein at the dose of 0.5 mg/kg mRNA. After 24 h, mice were administered an intraperitoneal injection of 10 μL/g of D-luciferin (15 mg/ml in DPBS). After 15 min, the mice were euthanized and perfused to remove the blood, and six organs were collected (lung, liver, spleen, heart, femur, and kidneys). The luminescence signal of each organ was analyzed using an IVIS imaging system (PerkinElmer IVIS Spectrum) and quantified using LivingImage software (PerkinElmer). The in vivo transfection efficiency of each dLNP formulation in these organs was quantified using total flux (p/s) in the tissue.

section_path: Materials and methods > Ex vivo imaging > Fluorescence Imaging:
text: B6.Cg-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J mice (Jackson Laboratories, 20-25 g) were intravenously injected with dLNPs (~100 μL for female and ~125 μL for male) via retro-orbital administration at the dose of 0.5 mg/kg Cre-recombinase mRNA on Day 0 and Day 1. After 48 h following the second injection, mice were euthanized and perfused. Following perfusion, six organs were collected (lung, liver, spleen, heart, femur, and kidneys). The fluorescent signal of each organ was analyzed using an IVIS imaging system (PerkinElmer IVIS Spectrum) and quantified using LivingImage software (PerkinElmer). The in vivo transfection efficiency of each dLNP formulation in these organs was quantified using average radiance (p/s/cm2/sr) in the tissue.

section_path: Materials and methods > Immunofluorescence study
text: B6.Cg-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J mice (Jackson Laboratories, 20-25 g) were intravenously injected with dLNPs (~100 μL for female and ~125 μL for male) via retro-orbital administration at the dose of 0.5 mg/kg Cre-recombinase mRNA on Day 0 and Day 1. After 48 h following the second injection, mice were euthanized and perfused. Following perfusion, the lungs, liver, and spleen were excised and transferred to a 4% w/v paraformaldehyde (PFA) buffered solution for 4 h at 4 °C. Following PFA fixation, samples were transferred to a 30% w/v sucrose solution for 24 h at 4 °C. Samples were then submitted the University of Florida Molecular Pathology Core (Gainesville, FL, USA) for OCT embedding and freezing, sectioning, and scanning. Images were generated using an Olympus VS200 Whole Slide Scanner and processed using OlyVIA software.

section_path: Materials and methods > Cell isolation and staining for flow cytometry
text: B6.Cg-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J mice (Jackson Laboratories, 20-25 g) were intravenously injected with dLNPs (~100 μL for female and ~125 μL for male) via retro-orbital administration at the dose of 0.5 mg/kg Cre-recombinase mRNA on Day 0 and Day 1. After 48 h following the second injection, mice were euthanized, and peripheral blood was collected via cardiac puncture. Following peripheral blood collection, mice were perfused, and the spleen and femur were collected.

section_path: Materials and methods > Cell isolation and staining for flow cytometry
text: For peripheral blood leukocyte isolation, mouse blood was collected via cardiac puncture using a 1 mL syringe coated with 0.5 M EDTA (Invitrogen). Approximately 250 μL of blood was transferred to a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube (Fisher Scientific) containing 100 μL 0.5 M EDTA (Invitrogen). Whole blood was centrifuged at 21 °C, 380 × g for 5 min.

section_path: Materials and methods > Cell isolation and staining for flow cytometry
text: For splenocyte isolation, spleens were collected post-perfusion and passed through a 50-μm filter using a pestle and HBSS (Gibco). The suspension was centrifuged at 4 °C, 380 × g for 5 min.

section_path: Materials and methods > Cell isolation and staining for flow cytometry
text: For bone marrow isolation, femurs were harvested and ends clipped with dissecting scissors after connective tissues were removed. The isolated femurs were placed in 0.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes with an 18G needle pierced bottom, cap removed, and tube nested within a secondary 1.5 microcentrifuge tube containing 100 μL HBSS (Gibco). Microcentrifuge tubes with femurs were centrifuged at 5700 RPM for 20 s at 21 °C to capture bone marrow.

section_path: Materials and methods > Cell isolation and staining for flow cytometry
text: All resulting cell pellets were resuspended with ACK lysis buffer (Gibco) to remove remaining red blood cells (RBCs) and subsequently diluted with FACS buffer (10% FBS + 1× HBSS). This RBC lysis cycle was repeated 1-2 times if RBCs persisted in sample. Single cells were then resuspended in cell staining buffer and added to flow tubes that contained antibodies (total volume 100 μL). The cells were incubated with antibodies for 30 min in the dark at room temperature. Cells were then washed with HBSS and resuspended in 0.5 μg/mL viability dye (Violet, Invitrogen). Samples were analyzed via a single flow cytometry tube on a Cytek Aurora spectral flow cytometer and data was processed using FlowJo software. Antibodies used were Spark Violet 538 anti-mouse CD45 (Biolegend, 103179), Brilliant Violet 711 anti-mouse CD11b (Biolegend, 101242), Brilliant Violet 605 anti-mouse Ly-6G (Biolegend, 127639), APC/Fire 750 anti-mouse Ly-6C (Biolegend, 128045), FITC anti-mouse CD11c (Biolegend, 117305), Brilliant Violet 421 anti-mouse F4/80 (Biolegend, 123137), PE/Cy7 anti-mouse CD3 (Biolegend, 100219), Alexa Fluor 647 anti-mouse CD19 (Biolegend, 115525), and PE/Cy5 anti-mouse Gr-1 (Biolegend, 108409).

section_path: Materials and methods > Bone marrow culture and transfection
text: Bone marrow-derived cells from wildtype C57BL/6 mice were prepared as previously described in published work [58]. Cells were then plated at a density of 400,000 cells/cm2 and concentration of 1000 cells/μL in media consisting complete RPMI (RPMI + 10% FBS + 2 mM L-Glutamine) supplemented with 40 ng/mL GM-CSF (R&D 415-ML) and 40 ng/mL IL-6 (R&D 406-ML). On day 3, the cells were centrifuged (150 × g, 3 min), the culture media replaced with 25% (v/v) mouse plasma (Innovative Research) in RPMI and then incubated with EGFP-mRNA encapsulating dLNPs for 3 h. After incubation, the cells were centrifuged, the nanoparticle-containing media removed, and fresh complete RPMI supplemented with GM-CSF and IL-6 added. After 24 h (Day 4), suspended cells were collected, the wells were washed in PBS and scraped using a cell scraper (Fisher), and all contents were joined together in a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube. Cells were collected via centrifugation (4 °C, 380 × g, 5 min) and processed for flow cytometry analysis. Antibodies used were Alexa Fluor 700 anti-mouse CD45 (Biolegend, 147716), Brilliant Violet 421 anti-mouse CD11b (Biolegend, 101251), PerCP anti-mouse Ly-6G (Biolegend, 127654), Brilliant Violet 785 anti-mouse Ly-6C (Biolegend, 128041). Viability was determined using Zombie NIR (Biolegend, 423105) dye.

section_path: Materials and methods > Statistical analysis
text: All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 10 (GraphPad Software). The statistical significance of observed differences between groups was assessed using an unpaired, two-tailed Studenťs t-test for pairwise comparisons or an unpaired, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for comparisons involving more than two groups. When ANOVA was used, Tukey’s post hoc test was applied to correct for multiple comparisons. All data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) unless otherwise specified. A P-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant, with significance levels indicated in corresponding figures or figure legends.
